title: Christ the Servant, the Gentiles' Praise, and Paul's Plans
summary: Paul completes his appeal to the strong and the weak: following Christ, who did not please himself, believers should bear with one another and welcome each other so that Jews and Gentiles glorify God together, as a chain of Scriptures foretold. He then explains his priestly calling to the Gentiles, his work from Jerusalem to Illyricum, and his plan to visit Rome on the way to Spain after delivering a collection to the poor believers in Jerusalem. He asks the Roman believers to pray for his safety and for the success of that mission.
story: The first thirteen verses finish the discussion that began in 14:1, grounding the call to mutual welcome in the example of Christ and in God's long purpose to bring the Gentiles to praise him alongside Israel. That purpose is the thread of the whole letter, announced in 1:5 and 1:16. From verse 14, Paul moves into the letter's closing, returning to the travel plans he mentioned in 1:10-15. He explains why he has written so boldly and why he has not yet come. The chapter shows the theology of Romans being lived out in a real mission, with real money, real dangers, and a real hope of reaching the western edge of the empire.
historical:
Paul wrote at a turning point in his work. He had preached in the eastern Mediterranean for more than two decades, planting churches in Syria, Asia Minor, Macedonia, and Greece. Illyricum was the Roman province along the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, north and west of Macedonia; Acts does not record a visit there, and Paul may mean he reached its border during his travels through Macedonia (Acts 20:1-2). Now he planned to go west to Spain, a long-established Roman province with no known church, and to use Rome as his base.

First, though, he was taking a collection from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the poor believers in Jerusalem, a project he describes also in 1 Corinthians 16 and 2 Corinthians 8 and 9. His fears in verse 31 proved well founded. Acts 21 records that he was attacked in the temple courts and arrested in Jerusalem, and he reached Rome some years later as a prisoner (Acts 28). Whether he ever reached Spain is uncertain. A letter from the church in Rome written around AD 96, known as 1 Clement, says Paul reached the farthest limits of the west, which some take to mean Spain, but the New Testament does not say.
cultural:
The collection had a meaning beyond charity. In the ancient world gifts created bonds and obligations between giver and receiver. By asking Gentile churches to give to the Jewish church in Jerusalem, Paul was making visible the unity of Jews and Gentiles in one people, and he interprets it as a debt: the Gentiles have shared in Israel's spiritual blessings, so they owe material help in return (verse 27). There was risk in the gift. Jerusalem believers might hesitate to accept money from uncircumcised Gentiles gathered by a controversial apostle, which is why Paul asks for prayer that it would be acceptable (verse 31).

Paul describes his mission in priestly terms. He calls himself a leitourgos, a minister in public or sacred service, doing the priestly work of the gospel, with the Gentiles themselves as the offering presented to God. In the Jerusalem temple, Gentiles could not go beyond the outer court. Paul pictures them offered to God and made holy by the Holy Spirit.
literary: Verses 1 to 13 form the conclusion of the argument begun in 14:1. They move from exhortation (verses 1-2) to Christ's example (verse 3, quoting Psalm 69:9) to a prayer (verses 5-6) to a renewed command (verse 7) to theological grounding (verses 8-9) and then to four Scripture quotations, from the Law (Deuteronomy 32:43), the Prophets (Isaiah 11:10), and the Writings (Psalm 18:49 and Psalm 117:1), all mentioning the Gentiles. Verse 13 is a benediction that gathers up the key words of the letter: hope, joy, peace, believing, and the power of the Spirit. The second half of the chapter (verses 14-33) is a travelogue in the style of ancient letters, explaining plans and requesting prayer, and it closes with another benediction.

outline.t: Bearing with the weak after Christ's example
Welcome one another: Jews and Gentiles praising God
Paul's priestly service to the Gentiles
Plans for Jerusalem, Rome, and Spain

doctrines.note: Paul understands his calling as bringing the Gentiles to the obedience of faith, and he aims to preach where Christ has not been named. The collection shows that mission includes practical care that binds churches together across ethnic lines.

Verse 4 states that what was written in the past was written for our instruction, so that we might have hope. Paul reads Israel's Scriptures as the living word of God addressed to the church, not simply as a record of the past.

God is called "the God of hope" (verse 13), and hope is linked to Scripture (verse 4), to the Gentiles' inclusion (verse 12), and to the power of the Spirit. Hope in Romans is not wishful thinking but confident waiting on God's promises.

words.note: Leitourgos, a minister or servant in public service. In the Greek world it described someone who performed a public duty, often at his own expense; in the Greek Old Testament it was used of priests and Levites serving at the sanctuary. Paul uses it to describe himself as a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, doing priestly service with the gospel.

Koinonia, fellowship, sharing, or partnership. In verse 26 it names the contribution for the poor in Jerusalem. For Paul the word joins spiritual communion and material sharing; the gift is itself an act of fellowship between Gentile and Jewish believers.

Elpis, hope. It appears three times in this chapter and frames the first half: the Scriptures give hope (verse 4), the Gentiles put their hope in the Root of Jesse (verse 12), and the God of hope fills believers so that they overflow with hope (verse 13).

christ: The chapter presents Christ as the servant who did not please himself. Paul applies Psalm 69:9 to him: the insults aimed at God fell on him. His self-giving is both the ground and the pattern of believers' care for one another. Verse 8 says Christ became a servant of the circumcised to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs, and verse 9 adds that his mission also brings the Gentiles to glorify God for his mercy. Christ is thus the fulfillment of God's faithfulness to Israel and of his mercy to the nations. He is "The Root of Jesse" (verse 12, quoting Isaiah 11:10), the promised descendant of David's father, who rules over the nations and in whom they hope. Paul's whole mission is described as what Christ has accomplished through him (verse 18).
questions: Christ did not please himself. Where are you being asked to set aside your own preferences for the good of someone else in your church?
Paul read the Old Testament as written for our instruction and hope. How does that change the way you might read it?
Paul's plans were real but uncertain, and he asked others to pray. How do you hold your own plans before God?
